newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan plans arresting more Bhutto loyalists.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan plans arresting more Bhutto loyalists.

text.p: More loyalists of Pakistan's ousted prime minister Benazir Bhutto may be arrested like her husband for allegedly conspiring to murder her estranged brother, a senior government official said on Friday.
"We will take action under the law...and will get all those who are responsible for the murder," Sindh province's caretaker Chief Minister Mumtaz Ali Bhutto told reporters.

Benazir's husband Asif Ali Zardari was re-arrested on Thursday on suspicion of involvement in the alleged murder of her brother Murtaza as soon as he was released from a Karachi jail after a court declared his six-week detention illegal.

Mumtaz said Abdullah Shah, former provincial chief minister and a Bhutto aide, had already obtained a pre-arrest bail in the murder case while Bhutto's former interior minister Naseerullah Babar would be arrested soon.
"The investigation is on and anything can happen," he said.

Murtaza's Lebanese-born widow Ghinwa, now chief of a breakaway faction of Benazir's Pakistan People's Party, has accused Zardari, Babar, Shah and some police officials of conspiring in the September 20 killing of her husband in a police shoot-out near his Karachi home.
Police say Murtaza was killed in crossfire after his bodyguards fired first at police.
A judicial tribunal is inquiring into the incident, which Benazir says was a conspiracy against her family and government, sacked on November 5 by President Farooq Leghari.
A police official, who asked not to be named, said Zardari would be presented before a magistrate on Saturday.
Leghari sacked Bhutto's government on November 5 on disputed charges of corruption and misrule.
Soon afterwards her husband was detained in the city of Lahore under the catch-all Maintenance of Public Order Ordinance.
Bhutto and Zardari have been at the centre of corruption allegations associated with the former government. Both deny any wrongdoing.

Bhutto and Murtaza had developed differences over rival claims to the leadership of the party founded by their father, former prime minister Zulfikar Ali Bhutto, who was toppled in an army coup in 1977 and hanged in 1979 after a controversial conviction for a murder conspiracy.
Murtaza returned from 16 years in exile in 1993 and last year set up his breakaway version of the PPP.
